claims.text: Adding 5–10 wt% Cu and applying controlled annealing will promote a continuous Cu-rich conduction network in the HEA.
The Cu-rich network will enhance heat-transfer capability without degrading structural integrity.
The baseline is a Cu-free, nominally refractory HEA with balanced strength and thermal stability.
Post-deposition annealing can produce a finely dispersed or continuous Cu-rich microstructure.
The proposed operating range is approximately 300–800 °C under significant cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
A Cu-rich phase will form along selected grain boundaries or as an interconnected network in the HEA.
The Cu-rich phase will remain mechanically bonded to the primary HEA matrix.
The Cu-rich phase will provide a high-electron-mobility pathway for thermal conduction.
Uniformly integrated and annealing-stabilized Cu can create local channels for enhanced heat transfer in an HEA.
The refractory, structurally robust HEA matrix will preserve load-bearing and creep-resistant properties at high temperature and under irradiation.
The Cu-alloyed and annealed HEA will exhibit a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity relative to the baseline.
The modified HEA will retain tensile strength and creep resistance comparable to the baseline under operational conditions.
Excess Cu or uncontrolled annealing may cause deleterious phase segregation and embrittlement.
The magnitude of conductivity improvement and the optimal Cu content and annealing parameters are not yet established.
Long-term microstructural stability and irradiation performance are not fully established.
Failure to increase thermal conductivity significantly, or any reduction in tensile strength, creep resistance, or phase stability, will falsify the hypothesis.
